title: Senate candidates looking to succeed Benson square off in Prince George’s forum
summary: Del. Tiffany Alston and Kevin Ford agreed on some issues, not on others, in a candidate forum just six weeks before the June 23 Democratic primary. As the only two candidates running to succeed Sen. Joanne C. Benson, the primary could be the ticket to the Senate.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters May 13, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters May 13, 2026

They disagreed on some issues, were more or less in agreement on more, but one thing can be said with near certainty about the two Democrats competing to succeed retiring Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince George’s) — the June 23 primary is the currently the only thing between them and that Senate seat.

Del. Tiffany Alston (D-Prince George’s) and Kevin Ford Jr. are not just the only two Democrats running for the District 24 Senate eat, they’re the only two candidates of any party, meaning the winner of the primary could waltz in unchallenged in the November general election.

The two met Tuesday night in a highly structured hourlong forum at the Collington retirement community in Mitchellville, where they answered two dozen questions on health, education, public safety and other topics. There were 13 questions for which they were allowed 60-second responses, five for 30 seconds eard and six “yes or no” questions with 15 seconds allowed for a brief answer.

The first question asked by Collington resident Elizabeth Gill, who served as the moderator: What is the first piece of legislation you would sponsor as senator?

Ford, a real estate broker, said it would be to limit the power of homeowner associations. He said he’s paying about $500 a month but “actually getting less back for what we’re paying.”

Happy birthday to the dean, the 411 on 311 on 3/11, and a standing invitation, in political notes

Alston, an attorney and first-term delegate, said she would sponsor legislation that’s been a hot-button topic in Annapolis for years: Supporting medical-aid-in dying legislation.

It’s a hot-button topic in Collington, too, where more than 300 residents signed a petition last year in support of the End of Life Option Act. The “aid in dying” bill sponsored by Del. Terri Hill (D-Howard), a plastic surgeon with a private practice since 1991, would have allowed terminally ill patients who me a number of criteria and safeguards to request that a physician prescribe a lethal dose of medication that the patient could take.

Aid-in-dying bills have been introduced without success for several years. Lawmakers said the stumbling block has been the Senate, which Alston reiterated Tuesday.

“The Senate has been way too conservative on this issue,” she said. “It is not in line with the values that we have as Marylanders to have choice over our bodies. We enshrined the rights of women in the constitution, but we left out the rights of people who are dying, and it is important and critical that we get this fixed now.”

The candidates were asked specifically if they would support legislation in the 2027 session. While Alston said she would sponsor the bill, Ford said he also supports the legislation, but “we have to have strong safeguards. We have to have physician oversight, and we need protection against coercion and abuse as well.”

The two candidates agreed that Maryland should invest to help people with drug or substance abuse and hold those manufacturing drugs accountable.

They disagreed on the effectiveness of public-private partnerships, also known as P3, achieve success when it comes to education infrastructure to build new schools through an accelerated timeline and reduce costs.

“I think the use of public private partnerships has been amazing,” Alston told the few dozen audience members. “We’ve now opened up investment opportunities where residents are able to invest in the infrastructure in the building, and I think those kinds of things are important.”

Ford said he would roll back the P3 program.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

“I think that we have to take longevity into account so that we are not spending unnecessary money, faster than we need to,” he said. “I do understand that it’s the expediency of everything that really attracts everybody to the P3s, but I think that we’re losing the longevity of our infrastructure in our schools by going this P3 route.”

The two are competing to replace Benson, who was first elected to the House in 199o and the Senate in 2021. Affectionately called “the dean” of the Senate, where she serves as majority whip, colleagues in both chambers honored her when she turned 85 in March. Besides Mitchellville, the district also includes Fairmount Heights, Glenarden and Lake Arbor.

The final question dealt with a bill Benson sponsored this year, Senate Bill 118, which proposed an 11% state excise tax on the sale of firearms, accessories and ammunition sold in the state by federally licensed  dealers. The fiscal note with the bill estimated it would generate about $11.4 million annually, starting in fiscal 2028. The money would be dedicated to six programs and centers that provide violence prevention and victims’ support services.

The bill never advanced beyond the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee.

The yes or no question asked to the candidates: “Will you honor our retiring senator by supporting this bill in 2027?”

“Absolutely, and I would also sponsor the legislation, too,” Ford said.

Alston’s response: “No, I don’t support the excise tax. I’m a supporter of the Second Amendment. I don’t feel like we should be taxing at every” turn.
